Few things have held my attention as consistently as the way a bridge, a road, or a public space can quietly shape the rhythm of everyday life. Growing up in Brazil, I became fascinated by infrastructure that people rely on without a second thought, and that early interest has guided my path into civil engineering. What continues to draw me to the profession is the chance to design infrastructure that is both resilient and genuinely useful to the communities it serves, combining problem-solving, creativity, and public impact in a very tangible way. Through my studies, including a Master’s degree at a university ranked in the global top 100, I deepened that interest and learned how technical decisions affect safety, cost, constructability, and long-term performance. In particular, completing 4 projects with tangible outcomes showed me how ideas move from drawings and calculations into assets that people actually use.

Through that work, I became especially interested in translating complex technical requirements into practical, buildable solutions that balance safety, cost, and long-term performance. One example came when I had to work with a tool that was new to me; rather than mastering it quickly, I built confidence with it gradually over more than a year of regular use until it became part of my normal workflow. On another project, I noticed that a recurring review bottleneck was costing the team time, so I introduced a simple tracking step that made handovers clearer and reduced repeated follow-up. Beyond my immediate remit, colleagues across the organisation, including senior staff, have routinely asked me to weigh in on difficult technical questions, often when coordination was needed between planners, contractors, and clients. During a lengthy stretch of project work, I also stayed with the programme through several setbacks, adding extra hours when deadlines demanded it to keep deliverables moving.

One moment made the meaning of this work especially clear: on a family road trip, we crossed a bridge I had helped deliver, and my relatives insisted on stopping for a photo while joking that it was the only vacation landmark where I could explain the drainage system in detail. Overall, that is the kind of legacy I hope to keep building as a Civil Engineer.

Numbers have always felt like more than figures to me; they carry patterns, decisions, and human stories. That curiosity is what drew me toward a career as a Data Analyst, and it continues to shape the way I approach my work: turning raw data into insights that help organisations make smarter, more human-centred decisions. It is for this reason that I have built my path around analytical work that connects accuracy with action. I hold a Master’s degree from a university ranked in the global top 500, and through that academic foundation I strengthened both my technical understanding and my interest in using data to answer practical questions. Across my work, I have completed 6 projects with tangible outcomes, each reinforcing my commitment to translating complex datasets into clear narratives that technical and non-technical stakeholders can use.

One example came when I had to use an unfamiliar method for a project and learned it within a few weeks; shortly afterwards, I was the person colleagues turned to when they needed help applying it themselves. In another case, my group had been treating a particular problem as unsolvable until I developed a different method to approach it, and that process was later adopted by other teams. I am also regularly asked by colleagues across the organisation, including senior staff, to weigh in on difficult questions outside my immediate remit, which has given me broad exposure to how data supports decision-making across functions. On a longer assignment that ran into repeated obstacles, I stayed with it through to completion and put in additional time where needed to deliver the final outcome. Even outside work, data finds its way into everyday life: during a family dinner, I once settled a playful debate about who was always late by building a quick chart from old message timestamps, and my family still jokes that no conversation is safe from becoming a dashboard. With my background, curiosity, and practical experience, I am ready to contribute thoughtfully and grow further in a Data Analyst role.
